scenario: Pre-registered review of SHAP and LIME on two synthetic invoice classifiers, same split, same cases, same outputs
intended_use: Engineering study only. Scores support review and are not proof of wrongdoing.

data.origin: Entirely synthetic fictional invoices with a known label-generating logit

assumptions_and_data.interventional_shap: Masked features take background values independently of the kept features. With dependent features the hybrid rows can be impossible combinations. The generator draws the six features independently, so the assumption matches this synthetic data; real invoices would need their dependence measured first.

lime_neighbourhood.definition: Continuous features: Gaussian noise with the training standard deviation around the case, not clipped. Binary features: resampled from the training frequencies, independently of the case. Weights: sqrt(exp(-d^2 / w^2)), d the Euclidean distance in LIME's design space.

preprocessing.method: StandardScaler fitted on the training rows only

interpretable_model.scale: class-1 log-odds per unit; odds ratios are exp(coefficient x increment)
interpretable_model.reading: Each coefficient is the change in class-1 log-odds for one unit of that input with the other inputs held fixed. The model has no interaction terms, so the change is the same at every value of the other inputs on the log-odds scale. It is an association learned from synthetic data, not a causal effect.
interpretable_model.correlation_limit: Coefficients hold the other inputs fixed. With correlated inputs that combination can be unrealistic and the coefficients become unstable; the correlation matrix and variance inflation factors measure how far that applies to these synthetic rows.

reference_case.reason: No bounded change of the mutable fields flips the decision.

reviewer_usefulness.reason: Requires people performing a task; no participant data exist.

proposed_study.task: Reviewers see synthetic invoice cases with the model score and decide the route (routine or review) and whether the score looks wrong. Conditions: score only, score with SHAP bars, score with LIME weights, score with a counterfactual. Some cases come from a deliberately corrupted model with one feature sign inverted.
proposed_study.participants: At least 12 accounts-payable or audit reviewers who did not build the model; within-subject design, conditions counterbalanced with a Latin square, cases randomised.
proposed_study.measures: Primary: detection rate of corrupted-model cases. Secondary: decision accuracy against the synthetic ground truth, forward-simulation accuracy, over-reliance rate on wrong scores, time per case, and a short trust and workload questionnaire.
proposed_study.analysis: Mixed-effects logistic regression with reviewer and case as random effects; effect sizes with 95 percent intervals; pre-registered before recruitment.

causality.reason: SHAP, LIME, coefficients and counterfactuals describe the fitted model, not the world. No causal claim is made.

limitations: Synthetic data, six numeric features and one 600/200 split do not establish usefulness on real invoices.
The label rule is linear, so the logistic model is correctly specified here; this is not a neutral comparison of model families.
Twenty cases selected by a stratified rule describe these cases, not every possible input.
Thresholds are illustrative values fixed before the run, not business, legal or production criteria.
Interventional SHAP assumes independent features; it matches this generator but must be checked on real data.
LIME's continuous perturbations are not clipped and can leave the schema bounds; its binary features are resampled from training frequencies.
SHAP-LIME agreement compares two explanations with each other, not with a known true attribution.
Counterfactuals describe the model's decision boundary, not advice or causal effects.
Reviewer usefulness and causality are not measured.
Durations describe this local CPU run, not production performance.

provenance.protocol_title: Explainability review: SHAP and LIME on the same models, cases and outputs
